title: Screening of high-strength subgenomic promoters of alphavirus replicase and their co-expression potential in saRNA vaccines.
abstract: Self-amplifying mRNA (saRNA) vaccines represent a promising platform for next-generation vaccines. However, their application is still limited by insufficient antigen expression and the difficulty of achieving precise multi-gene regulation in multivalent vaccine designs. Subgenomic promoters (SGPs) derived from Alphavirus replicase play a critical role in regulating downstream gene transcription and therefore provide an attractive target for promoter engineering. In this study, the 24 nt core sequence of the Alphavirus SGP was targeted for optimization. A randomized mutation library was constructed and screened using a high-throughput fluorescence detection system based on enhanced green fluorescent protein (EGFP) as a reporter. Candidate promoters were subsequently validated through sequencing analysis and cellular expression assays. A total of 20 novel SGP variants with enhanced transcriptional activity were successfully identified. Among them, the 9 G → T mutant showed the most prominent improvement in expression performance. Semi-quantitative fluorescence analysis confirmed that several mutant promoters significantly accelerated the onset of target protein expression and increased overall expression levels compared with the wild-type promoter. RNA secondary structure prediction further suggested that the enhanced promoter activity may be associated with alterations in local stem-loop conformations within the SGP region. In addition, co-transfection assays further demonstrated that the 9 G → T mutant maintains favorable co-expression compatibility with the wild-type SGP, indicating its potential utility in multigene expression systems. These findings provide a set of high-strength subgenomic promoters and an effective screening strategy for saRNA systems, offering practical regulatory elements for improving antigen expression and facilitating the development of multivalent saRNA vaccines.

title: RNA ensembles: From sequence to cellular function.
abstract: Advances in structure prediction have transformed biology, yet static structures alone cannot quantitatively predict binding affinities, reaction rates, or how cellular activity changes with sequence. Modeling and ultimately predicting these properties requires describing RNAs as ensembles of interconverting conformations, whose populations are reshaped by interactions with cellular factors to control function. Here, we review recent advances in defining these RNA conformational ensembles and incorporating them into causal, predictive models of RNA molecular behavior and cellular activity. Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), chemical probing, cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), X-ray crystallography, atomic force microscopy (AFM), and computation are extending ensemble analysis to larger RNAs, complex assemblies, cellular environments, and biomedical applications. Together, these developments reveal conformational ensembles as an essential quantitative bridge linking RNA sequence, biochemical activity, and cellular function.

title: SCOPE: Single-Cell Omics Prediction from Histology via RNA-Protein Prior Enhancement
abstract: Predicting the RNA and protein content of cells from routine H&E images could extend spatial molecular profiling to existing slide archives. However, both H&E-spatial proteomics and H&E-spatial transcriptomics paired datasets are limited by the number of available markers and the insufficient availability of high-quality, cell-resolved data. We present SCOPE (Single-Cell Omics Prediction via RNA-protein prior Enhancement), a unified framework that leverages biologically complementary information between RNA and proteins to address the limited availability of single-omics supervision. Our key insight is that, although RNA and proteins represent distinct molecular modalities, their biological relationships provide valuable shared knowledge that can benefit single-omics prediction tasks. To this end, SCOPE introduces biologically informed biomarker priors to enhance shared gene-level representations, enabling knowledge transfer across RNA and protein modalities through gene-protein correspondence and molecular associations. By exploiting these complementary relationships, SCOPE enables both prediction tasks to benefit from a shared backbone enriched with cross-omics biological knowledge. Furthermore, its biomarker correlation design facilitates the prediction of unseen markers, extending spatially resolved molecular profiling beyond directly supervised targets. Across test datasets spanning 16 organs, SCOPE improves the average RNA Pearson correlation over the strongest baseline by 8.8%. On two external protein cohorts, it improves the average Pearson correlation over the strongest baseline by 9.7% for seen markers and 11.9% for unseen markers.

title: Deltacoronavirus modulates circRNA circC3 biogenesis to accelerate MBNL1 mRNA decay.
abstract: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) with diverse biological functions are frequently dysregulated upon viral infection, yet the mechanisms governing their differential expression and functional relevance during infection remain poorly defined. Here, we identify a previously uncharacterized circRNA, circC3, that is robustly upregulated following virus infection. Host RNA binding protein muscleblind-like 1 (MBNL1) was markedly induced by deltacoronavirus (δ-CoV) infection, which recognizes YGCY motifs within intron 19 and intron 21 of the C3 gene and promotes skipping of exons 20 and 21 for C3 gene, thereby enhancing circC3 biogenesis. These findings reveal an MBNL1-dependent mechanism underlying δ-CoV induced circC3 upregulation. Functionally, circC3 attenuates the antiviral activity of MBNL1 by accelerating MBNL1 mRNA decay through a direct interaction, and finally promote δ-CoV replication. Together, our study elucidates a regulatory circuit in which viral infection remodels host circRNA biogenesis to counteract antiviral defenses, highlighting circC3 as a potential target for antiviral intervention.

title: Prediction of lncRNA-cervical cancer associations using a multi-view collaborative variational autoencoder with knowledge distillation transfer learning.
abstract: Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) play critical regulatory roles in the pathogenesis of cervical cancer, and accurate identification of lncRNA-cervical cancer associations is important for understanding the molecular mechanisms of the disease and discovering potential therapeutic targets. However, the extreme scarcity of cervical cancer-specific lncRNA association data constitutes a major bottleneck limiting the performance of existing computational prediction methods. To address this challenge, we propose a Multi-View Collaborative Variational Autoencoder based on Knowledge Distillation Transfer Learning (MVCVAE), which integrates multi-source heterogeneous data fusion and cross-disease knowledge transfer in a task-oriented manner. The multi-view collaborative variational autoencoder constructs dual-view feature representations of lncRNA and disease similarities and employs a symmetric encoder-decoder architecture to learn complex lncRNA-disease association patterns in the latent space. The knowledge distillation transfer learning framework adopts a teacher-student network design: a teacher model is pre-trained on a large-scale dataset containing 12,865 lncRNA-disease associations to learn general association patterns, and the resulting prior knowledge is effectively transferred to a student model targeting 92 cervical cancer associations through feature distillation and prediction distillation strategies. In five-fold cross-validation, MVCVAE achieves an AUC of 0.9228 ± 0.0058. Through the synergistic effects of multi-view heterogeneous information fusion and cross-domain knowledge transfer, MVCVAE demonstrates strong performance in predicting lncRNA-cervical cancer associations, effectively addressing the limitations imposed by the scarcity of cervical cancer-specific lncRNA association data.

title: Identification of marker genes and signaling pathways associated with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis using bioinformatics analysis of RNA sequencing data.
abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), is a global disease that is a leading cause of neurodegenerative condition that affects motor neurons. However, the etiology of ALS remains poorly understood. The genes responsible for the pathogenesis of ALS have not been fully identified. To identify novel genes associated with carcinogenesis and progression of PDA, we analyzed the RNA sequencing dataset GSE277709 from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database. The differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified using DESeq2 R bioconductor package, whereas the Gene Ontology (GO) and REACTOME pathway enrichment analysis were performed by g:Profiler. Protein-protein interaction (PPI) network of DEGs was analyzed by HIPPIE (Human Integrated Protein-Protein Interaction rEference) interactome online database, and Cytoscape software was used for visualizing PPI network. Then, the microRNAs (miRNAs) and transcription factors (TF) in ALS were screened out from the miRNet and NetworkAnalyst database. Potential drug targets for ALS were obtained from the DrugBank database. MiRNA-hub gene regulatory network, TF-hub gene regulatory network and drug-hub gene interaction network were constructed by Cytoscape software. Finally, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was performed to assess the diagnostic value of hub genes. There exist strong correlations among samples of ALS and normal control group. There was a total of 958 DEGs, including 479 up-regulated genes and 479 down-regulated genes. GO enrichment analysis revealed that these DEGs were associates with multicellular organismal process, primary metabolic process, cell periphery, intracellular membraneless organelle, signaling receptor and transmembrane transporter activity. REACTOME pathway enrichment analysis revealed that these DEGs were associates with extracellular matrix organization and sensory perception. Hub genes EGFR (epidermal growth factor receptor), FN1 (fibronectin 1), CAV1 (caveolin 1), BCAR1 (BCAR1 scaffold protein, Cas family member), YAP1 (Yes1 associated transcriptional regulator), POU5F1 (POU class 5 homeobox 1), TTYH1 (tweety family member 1), ACTA1 (actin alpha 1, skeletal muscle), GPR17 (G protein-coupled receptor 17) and TF (transferrin) were identified form PPI network and modules. The MiRNA-hub gene regulatory network and TF-hub gene regulatory network showed that hsa-miR-6874-5p, hsa-miR-561-5p, GATA2 (GATA binding protein 2) and SRF (serum response factor) might play an important role in the ALS. By analyzing drug-hub gene interaction network, we pridicted drug molecules such as Lormetazepam and Medazepam for ALS treatment. These hubs demonstrated strong diagnostic values. The study highlights the potential impact of EGFR, FN1, CAV1, BCAR1, YAP1, POU5F1, TTYH1, ACTA1, GPR17 and TF on the development and progression of ALS, supporting their role as potential biomarkers.

title: Genome-wide identification and analysis of RNA secondary structures in response to glucose in Plasmodium falciparum.
abstract: Food intake has a significant effect on systemic physiology. The growth, development and transmission of malaria-causing Plasmodium parasites rely on carbohydrate utilization, and parasites must rapidly adapt to fluctuating host glucose concentrations throughout their life cycle. However, the precise process by which Plasmodium parasites quickly react and adapt to glucose stress, in general, remains elusive. The goal of this investigation was to determine whether glucose starvation affects the RNA secondary structure of parasites. In this study, we applied different short-term glucose stresses on parasites to determine the effect of host-derived glucose nutrients on the dynamics of parasite development and RNA secondary structures. We found that the S-type rRNA expression level in the low glucose-treated group was higher than that in the 2 mg/mL control group. The RNA-seq results indicated that glucose significantly affects the expression of genes involved in RNA-related processes, antigenic variation, transport processes, stimulus response, and DNA-related activities. Metabolomics studies also revealed that several types of sugar compounds exhibit a decrease in metabolic activity when subjected to a reduction in glucose supply. Via analysis of three glucose conditions, we identified the RNA secondary structures of more than 2,721 transcripts throughout the intraerythrocytic trophozoite stage. We discovered a positive correlation between mRNA structural flexibility (icSHAPE scores) and transcript abundance (RPKM values), demonstrating a direct association between RNA structural openness and steady-state mRNA levels. Our results revealed structural alterations in the entire transcriptome, including glucose transporters, metabolic enzymes, and the erythrocyte invasion protein family. These genes were mainly enriched in response to stimuli or preferential biological processes. The total number of genes with changes in icSHAPE scores in the UTRs was significantly greater for the 3' UTRs than the 5' UTRs. Furthermore, by comparing icSHAPE reactivity profiles across glucose conditions, we identified candidate cis-acting RNA motifs predominantly located within UTRs, whose structural flexibility changed rapidly in response to glucose fluctuation. We term these glucose-responsive RNA motifs, as they constitute promising regulatory elements for future research into post-transcriptional glucose sensing mechanisms. Our findings clarify glucose stress-triggered remodeling of in vivo RNA secondary structure during the P. falciparum intraerythrocytic stage, reveal the functional relevance of structural dynamics in parasite environmental adaptation, and lay a foundational resource for future nutrient stress and post-transcriptional regulatory research. These findings show that glucose, the primary carbon source for parasite survival, modulates RNA secondary structural dynamics via nutrient-sensing cascades to modulate parasite proliferation and adaptive development, which offers clues for developing novel antimalarial therapies.

title: The fate of poised pre-mRNAs shapes mitochondrial activity and cellular differentiation.
abstract: Although RNA quality control tightly regulates gene expression, the scope of its regulatory functions in the nucleus remains unclear. In this study, we describe the quality control, on chromatin, of poised intron-containing polyadenylated RNAs (PIA-RNAs). Whether these precursor messenger RNAs (pre-mRNAs) constitute immature mRNAs whose splicing is pending or, alternatively, are degraded by the nuclear RNA exosome depends on whether they engage nuclear cap-binding protein 3 (NCBP3) or anillin, respectively. Many PIA-RNAs inversely controlled by NCBP3 and anillin encode mitochondrial factors. Thus, NCBP3 depletion in mouse as well as pathogenic mutations in the RNA exosome in humans result in reduced mitochondrial activity, muscle weakness, cerebellar hypomyelination, and diminished motor coordination. Our findings reveal a competition between pre-mRNA metabolic pathways whose balance controls mitochondrial function and, when perturbed, leads to neurological diseases.

title: N6-methyladenosine dependent glycolysis enhances viral infection by histone lactylation in an arthropod.
abstract: The glycolysis is crucial for the material and energy source of virus infection. However, the role of post-transcriptional modification, particularly N6-methyladenosine (m6A), in regulating virus-induced glycolysis in invertebrate remains unclear. Here, we demonstrate that METTL3-mediated m6A modification of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) mRNA increased in shrimp upon white spot syndrome virus (WSSV) infection to promote glycolysis. An m6A site in the LDH mRNA is recognized by the m6A reader YTH domain family protein 3 (YTHDF3), which recruits translation initiation factor core subunit eIF4A to enhance LDH translation elongation and mRNA stability. LDH-derived lactate acts as a key metabolite responsible for lactylation of histone lysine residues that stimulates methyltransferase-like 3 (mettl3) gene transcription from chromatin directly. High levels of METTL3 were responsible for the upregulation of LDH, thereby facilitating lactate production by glycolysis. In summary, our results demonstrate that m6A and lactate function as viral responders, revealing a mechanistic link between RNA epitranscriptomic regulation and metabolic reprogramming, and establishes an indispensable role of histone lactylation, which performs to connect innate immunity and metabolism in the condition of virus infection.

title: Co-translational surveillance of nascent polypeptides times circadian rhythms in Drosophila.
abstract: Ribosome-associated quality control (RQC) ensures proteostasis by actively degrading aberrant translation intermediates on stalled ribosomes, yet its physiological role in gene regulation remains elusive. Here, we demonstrate that Drosophila circadian clocks employ RQC to sustain 24-h behavioral rhythms. RNA interference-mediated depletion of RQC components in circadian pacemaker neurons impaired free-running locomotor rhythms. In particular, the loss of Caliban (Clbn) function in clearing 60S-associated faulty polypeptides led to weak but long-period rhythms in adult locomotor activity. These behavioral phenotypes were accompanied by delayed accumulation of the core clock protein PERIOD (PER), most evidently in pigment-dispersing factor-expressing clock neurons, and dampened structural plasticity of their axons. per heterozygosity exaggerated CLBN depletion-induced period lengthening, whereas overexpression of the PER-associating factor TIMELESS blunted this effect. Clbn deficiency in Drosophila S2R+ cell cultures increased the generation of prematurely terminated PER species, particularly when PER translation is high, and sensitized full-length PER to phosphorylation-dependent decay. These findings support PER as a clock-relevant RQC substrate, providing a mechanistic link between translation flux, co-translational surveillance, and circadian timekeeping.
extra: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A

title: Authentic structure of the CCHFV RNA-nucleoprotein complex at near-atomic resolution.
abstract: Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) poses a major public health threat without approved vaccines or antivirals. Its ribonucleoprotein (RNP) is essential for replication, but its native architecture and RNA packaging remain elusive. Here, we combine AI-based structural prediction with cryo-electron microscopy to resolve the native structure of the CCHFV RNP purified from CCHFV-infected cells. We report a 3.87 Å structure of a single-turn RNP, and local refinement yielded a 3.55 Å structure of two adjacent NP protomers with continuous RNA. This represents the highest-resolution authentic RNP structure reported among segmented negative-strand RNA viruses (sNSVs), and provides the structural basis for CCHFV RNP assembly. Together with mutational analyses, these findings define the molecular basis of RNA encapsidation and NP oligomerization in the native CCHFV RNP. Our findings provide a hybrid structural framework integrating AI and experimental approaches for understanding genome organization in sNSVs and offer a foundation for future antiviral development.
extra: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A

title: Ribosome stalling activates a conserved quality control pathway in Archaea.
abstract: Ribosome stalling caused by defective mRNAs or translational stress can generate incomplete polypeptides and compromise ribosome availability. Although ribosome-associated quality control (RQC) pathways are well characterized in eukaryotes and bacteria, their presence in Archaea remains unexplored. Here, we established a programmable ribosome stalling system in the archaeon Sulfolobus acidocaldarius and used it to characterize the associated quality control machinery. Stalled ribosomes recruit the conserved NEMF/Rqc2 homolog aRqc2 together with the ribosome rescue factors aPelota and ABCE1. Proteomic and genetic analyses further identify the kinase-ATPase Rio2 and a previously uncharacterized archaeal factor, aRqcF, as candidate components of archaeal RQC. Stalled ribosome complexes also associate with RNA-processing factors, the archaeal exosome, and the proteasome-associated machinery, linking ribosome surveillance to RNA and protein quality control. Finally, we show that a short C-terminal alanine-rich sequence is sufficient to destabilize a reporter protein in S. acidocaldarius, demonstrating that alanine-rich sequences can function as degradation-promoting signals in Archaea. These findings suggest that archaeal RQC shares fundamental features with bacterial and eukaryotic systems, supporting an evolutionarily conserved principle of ribosome surveillance and quality control across the three domains of life. Ribosome-associated quality control (RQC) is essential for maintaining proteome integrity when translation is interrupted, yet how this pathway operates in Archaea remains poorly understood. Here, we establish a programmable in vivo system in the Archaeon Sulfolobus acidocaldarius and use it to define conserved and archaea-specific features of ribosome surveillance. By bridging a central evolutionary divide, this work provides new insight into the origin and diversification of translational quality control mechanisms that safeguard proteome integrity. In addition, it establishes S. acidocaldarius as a versatile experimental model for investigating archaeal RQC and its evolution.

title: Ultrahigh-Dose-Rate Radiation Therapy Spares Lymphocytes and Increases T cell Infiltration in Human Papillomavirus-Positive Tumors.
abstract: Radiation therapy (RT) delivered at conventional dose rates (CONV RT) can both stimulate antitumor immune responses and inhibit them by depleting circulating lymphocytes. Given the observed normal tissue sparing associated with ultrahigh-dose-rate (FLASH) RT, we hypothesized that it may protect lymphocytes while increasing the immunogenicity of human papillomavirus (HPV)-positive tumors. We irradiated HPV-positive cancer cell lines, TC-1 and mEER, in vitro with either FLASH RT or CONV RT and assessed immunogenic messenger RNA and protein expression; we also irradiated tumors in syngeneic C57BL/6 mice with 27 Gy in 3 fractions with FLASH RT or CONV RT and assessed changes in lymphocyte populations. Both cell lines showed upregulation of Calr, Hmgb1, and cGAS-STING family members after FLASH RT but not after CONV RT in vitro. In tumor-bearing mice treated with FLASH-RT, tumor-draining lymph nodes had greater numbers of CD8+ T cells (1.7 × 104 vs 0.8 × 104 CONV RT; P < .001) and CD4+ T cells (2.3 × 104 vs 1.2 × 104 CONV RT; P < .001). FLASH RT was also associated with an increased number of antigen-experienced CD44+CD62LloCD8+ and CD4+ lymphocytes. In irradiated tumors, FLASH RT was associated with increased CD8+ tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, increased program cell death protein 1 (PD-1) expression on these lymphocytes, and increased programmed death-ligand 1 expression on macrophages. Compared with CONV RT, FLASH RT spared antigen-experienced effector-like T cells in tumors and in tumor-draining lymph nodes, but showed higher intratumoral CD8+ T cell counts with increased checkpoint inhibitor PD-1 expression. These results indicate that FLASH RT preserves lymphocyte numbers while maintaining radiation-induced immunogenic signaling, suggesting that FLASH RT supports antitumor responses in HPV-positive cancer models. This response may be further amplified by combining FLASH RT with immune checkpoint blockade.

title: Sugarcane mosaic virus HC-Pro-triggered hypersensitive cell death is modulated by interaction with P3N-PIPO.
abstract: Sugarcane mosaic virus (SCMV) causes heavy yield losses in both sugarcane and maize. However, the hypersensitive cell death (HCD) induced by SCMV helper component proteinase (HC-Pro), an RNA silencing suppressor (RSS), has not been characterized. Here, we show that transient expression of HC-Pro of sugarcane isolate (SCMVSc), but not HC-ProZm of maize isolate (SCMVZm), induces dose-dependent HCD in Nicotiana benthamiana and other plant species. HC-Pro-induced HCD is independent of salicylic acid, reactive oxygen species, and receptor kinases BAK1/SOBIR1, but dependent on Ca2+ influx and helper nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat receptors ADR1/N NRG1. The conserved F345 in HC-Pro is key to HCD induction, whereas the corresponding residue in HC-ProZm is Y345. HC-ProZmY345F induces HCD in N. benthamiana leaves. Correspondingly, SCMVZm-HC-ProY345F-GFP demonstrated markedly decreased infectivity on N. benthamiana and maize compared with SCMVZm-GFP. Furthermore, we show that the interaction between SCMVSc movement protein P3N-PIPO and HC-Pro enhances the RSS activity of HC-Pro and inhibits the intercellular diffusion of silencing signals and HC-Pro-induced HCD, and that the RSS activity of HC-Pro is not required for HCD induction. Together, these findings reveal that SCMV employs different strategies to circumvent HC-Pro-induced HCD in plants, shedding light on the co-evolution mechanisms between SCMV and its hosts sugarcane and maize.

title: Competing Effects Modulate the Rate of Poly(A) RNA Deadenylation in a Biomolecular Condensate.
abstract: The unique solvent milieu found in biomolecular condensates can control cellular enzymatic reactions and shift reaction kinetics by modulating reactant concentrations, structural dynamics, and enzyme activities. Here, we explore the interplay of multiple regulatory factors within a condensate to control poly(A) RNA deadenylation, the first and rate-limiting step in mRNA turnover. The deadenylase CNOT7, a subunit of the CCR4-NOT deadenylation complex, localizes to protein- and RNA-rich granules and shows increased degradation activity in vitro in condensates formed by the C-terminal low-complexity disordered region of CAPRIN1, a component of many ribonucleoprotein (RNP) granules. We use a combination of enzymatic assays, kinetic modeling, microscopy, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, and molecular dynamics simulations to deconvolute and define the components that underlie this enhancement. We found that enzyme and RNA are concentrated in condensates relative to buffer, which increases CNOT7 activity, while the equilibrium between CNOT7's active and inactive states remains unchanged. The concentration-dependent increase in enzymatic rates is counterbalanced by a decrease in the enzyme's catalytic efficiency, likely due to slower diffusion of CNOT7 and RNA within the condensates, which lessens the probability of enzyme-substrate complex formation. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal CNOT7-CAPRIN1 interactions that rely on conserved CAPRIN1 sequence features, hinting at an evolutionarily conserved role for CAPRIN1 condensation. With this quantitative kinetic analysis, we describe the multifaceted mechanism behind regulation of CNOT7 deadenylation by a condensate environment.

title: Stress Granules in Health and Disease: From Adaptive RNA Triage to Pathological Persistence.
abstract: Stress granules (SGs) are cytoplasmic ribonucleoprotein (RNP) condensates that assemble when translation initiation is inhibited during stress. Classically viewed as transient sites of mRNA triage, SGs are now recognized as heterogeneous assemblies whose composition, material properties, and recovery capacity vary with the stressor, cell type, RNA substrate, and clearance pathway. SG assembly involves the selective recruitment of untranslated RNPs, followed by nucleation and maturation. SG disassembly is an active process in which translational restart, protein remodeling, and degradative pathways influence whether SG components return to function or are targeted for degradation. In neurodegenerative disease, prolonged residence of SG-associated RNAs and proteins may prevent their return to normal function and favor persistent or aberrant RNP states. In this Review, we propose that SGs are more informatively defined by mechanism and molecular state than by marker positivity alone. We organize SG biology along a continuum from acute, adaptive RNA triage to chronic, persistent SG-like assemblies. This framework helps reconcile the distinct relationships between SGs and different neurodegenerative diseases. It also distinguishes persistent, poorly resolved SG-like states as potential disease-relevant targets from physiological SGs that function as adaptive stress-response compartments.

title: Chromosome-level genome assembly of Ceroplastes rusci Linnaeus, 1758 (Hemiptera: Coccidae).
abstract: The fig wax scale, Ceroplastes rusci (Linnaeus, 1758), is a polyphagous, globally invasive pest native to Africa, causing severe economic losses. High-quality genomic resources for this species are lacking, limiting molecular research on its biology and management. Here, we report a high-quality chromosome-level genome assembly of C. rusci, with a total length of 426.70 Mb and a scaffold N50 of 24.19 Mb. Hi-C data anchored 99.96% of the assembly into 18 chromosomes. The genome contains 11,587 protein-coding genes (95.71% functionally annotated) with a BUSCO completeness of 95.3% (hemiptera_odb12). Repetitive elements account for 55.48% of the genome, of which 50.61% are unclassified repeats; among classified repetitive elements, LTR retrotransposons represent the dominant category. We also annotated 996 non-coding RNA loci and characterized SSRs and transposable elements. This chromosome-scale genome provides a key resource for studying the evolution, host adaptation, insecticide resistance, reproductive strategies, and symbiotic interactions of scale insects, and will support the development of precise monitoring and sustainable control strategies against this invasive pest.

title: ZCCHC4 promotes replication-dependent histone mRNA translation through interaction with the eIF3 complex.
abstract: Histone synthesis is tightly coupled with DNA replication to ensure proper chromatin assembly and genome stability. To meet the sharply elevated demand for histones during S phase, eukaryotic cells employ specialized mechanisms to translate replication-dependent (RD) histone mRNAs. These mRNAs possess distinctive features, such as specific UTR structures and the absence of poly(A) tails. Nevertheless, the molecular mechanisms controlling the translation of RD-histone mRNAs remain incompletely understood. In the current study, we report that ZCCHC4, which has been identified as the m6A RNA methyltransferase for 28S rRNA, is a novel regulator essential for RD-histone mRNA translation. ZCCHC4 exhibits unexpected subcellular localization of cytoplasm besides nucleus, and the cytoplasmic ZCCHC4 directly interacts with components of the translation initiation machinery. Depletion of ZCCHC4 reduces global protein translation, particularly the translation of RD histones. This translational impairment leads to insufficient histone supply, chromatin relaxation, and prolongs the S phase of the cell cycle. Moreover, ZCCHC4 knockout markedly inhibits cell proliferation, colony-forming ability, and the growth of xenograft tumors. Collectively, this study establishes a previously unrecognized role for ZCCHC4 in histone synthesis, at least in part through its interaction with eIF3, thereby sustaining histone supply during S phase in tumor cells. Our findings not only provide novel insights into histone mRNA translation control but also point to a potential role for ZCCHC4 in tumorigenesis.

title: Machine learning-integrated full-length 16S rRNA gene profiling reveals early-life gut microbial signatures associated with subsequent infantile colic in Thai infants.
abstract: Infantile colic develops after the neonatal period, but neonatal gut microbial patterns preceding symptom onset remain unclear. We examined early-life gut microbiome associations with subsequent infantile colic and internally evaluated microbiome-only prediction alongside retrospective metadata-containing comparisons. Stool samples collected 0-4 days after birth from 209 Thai infants (119 healthy and 90 who later met Rome IV diagnostic criteria for infantile colic) were profiled by Oxford Nanopore full-length 16S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) gene sequencing. Analyses included diversity and composition assessments, covariate-adjusted MaAsLin3 models, repeated nested cross-validation, and exploratory conditional association networks. Infants who subsequently developed infantile colic had lower Chao1 richness than healthy infants (q = 8.7 × 10-5), although delivery mode and collection day explained more community variation than outcome status. After covariate adjustment, Enterococcus faecium presence was associated with subsequent colic (odds ratio, 4.23; q = 0.021). The fully nested model-development procedure yielded participant-level area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) values of 0.773 and 0.740. In a secondary fixed-model comparison including feeding summarized through one month, a species-presence radial basis function support vector machine outperformed metadata alone (mean outer-fold AUROC/AUPRC, 0.780/0.764 vs. 0.539/0.484), while adding metadata produced only a small, uncertain improvement. Exploratory network analysis contextualized candidate taxa within group-specific conditional association modules. These findings support a focused early-life species-level pattern associated with subsequent infantile colic and prioritize candidate microbial features for external validation.

title: N6-methyladenosine-mediated down regulation of hsa_circ_0002420 promotes macrophage M1 polarisation in sepsis by regulating the miR-5586-5p/RAD23B axis.
abstract: Macrophage polarisation plays a crucial role in sepsis-associated inflammatory responses; however, the underlying molecular regulatory mechanisms remain to be further explored. This study aimed to explore the role of circ_0002420 in regulating macrophage polarisation. Quantification of key molecules was performed using reverse transcription-quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) for mRNAs, western blotting for proteins and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay for secreted proteins. The genomic locus of circ_0002420 was validated via Sanger sequencing. The stability of circ_0002420 was assessed after RNase R digestion and actinomycin D treatment. CD80-, CD86- and CD206-positive cells were detected via flow cytometry. Molecular interactions were verified using RNA immunoprecipitation, dual-luciferase reporter and miRNA pull-down assays. The m6A modification was detected via a methylated RNA immunoprecipitation assay. Circ_0002420 was down regulated in peripheral blood mononuclear cells from patients with sepsis-induced lung injury and in M1 macrophages. Mechanistically, methyltransferase-like 3-mediated m6A modification recruited YTH N6-methyladenosine RNA binding protein F2 to suppress circ_0002420 expression. Circ_0002420 directly sponged miR-5586-5p to modulate its availability. MiR-5586-5p targeted RAD23 nucleotide excision repair protein B (RAD23B) mRNA and suppressed its expression. Circ_0002420 overexpression inhibited M1 polarisation and inflammation through mediating the miR-5586-5p/RAD23B axis. The circ_0002420/miR-5586-5p/RAD23B axis regulates macrophage M1 polarisation and inflammatory responses, providing insights into sepsis-associated macrophage inflammation.

title: The box C/D snoRNP assembly factor Bcd1 binds the Ty1 retrotransposon capsid protein Gag and regulates retrotransposition.
abstract: Small nucleolar RNAs (snoRNAs) are key components of ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes that are best known for coordinating the folding, processing, and chemical modification of ribosomal RNAs. Biogenesis of these complexes requires dedicated assembly factors, yet whether such factors participate in processes beyond snoRNP formation remains poorly understood. Here, we identify an unexpected connection between box C/D snoRNP biogenesis and retrotransposition in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. We show that the essential box C/D snoRNP assembly factor Bcd1 directly binds the Ty1 structural protein Gag. In addition to Bcd1, core box C/D snoRNP factors associate with Gag, indicating that this interaction occurs within a broader snoRNP-associated context. Consistent with this observation, a subset of Bcd1- and Nop58-containing complexes co-migrate with a distinct RNA-dependent lower-molecular-weight Gag-containing population that is biochemically separable from viral-like particle assemblies. Direct binding of Bcd1 alters the proteolytic accessibility of Gag, suggesting that Bcd1 association influences the biochemical properties of the protein. Disruption of box C/D snoRNP biogenesis weakens the association of Gag with both Bcd1 and Nop58 and is accompanied by increased Ty1 retrotransposition. Together, our findings identify Bcd1 as a direct Gag-binding factor, reveal an association of Gag with box C/D snoRNP-associated complexes, and uncover a previously unrecognized connection between snoRNP biogenesis and Ty1 retrotransposition.

title: Spliceosomal intron-free eukaryotic cells: rethinking the evolutionary significance of introns and the spliceosome.
abstract: Spliceosomal introns are important components of eukaryotic genomes, occurring widely within protein-coding genes and being removed through splicing during RNA maturation. Spliceosomal intron removal has long been considered an important foundation of eukaryotic gene expression regulation and cellular function, and has also been proposed as a potential driver of eukaryotic evolution. All extant free-living eukaryotes are known to contain spliceosomal introns. However, whether introns and the spliceosome are essential for the survival of eukaryotic cells remains a fundamental question in biology. In recent years, advances in synthetic biology and genome engineering have provided new strategies for exploring the fundamental components of eukaryotic life. Through synthetic genome design and systematic genome minimization, recent studies have demonstrated that Saccharomyces cerevisiae can survive in the complete absence of all known spliceosomal introns, indicating that spliceosomal introns are not genetic elements essential for yeast viability, and that the spliceosome is likewise not a molecular machine required for yeast survival. This finding challenges the conventional understanding of spliceosomal intron function and spliceosome essentiality, provides a new perspective on the evolutionary significance of introns, and offers guiding principles for the rational design and construction of synthetic eukaryotic genomes. This review systematically summarizes the types and multifaceted functions of introns, with a focus on the construction, viability, and fitness cost of the spliceosomal intron-free Saccharomyces cerevisiae strain SYNE27α, as well as evidence that the spliceosome is dispensable in this context. It further discusses the implications for the evolutionary retention of introns and the construction of minimal eukaryotic genomes.

title: Targeting neutral sphingomyelinase enhances NK cell-mediated immunity via the CXCL10-CXCR3 axis in murine bladder cancer cells.
abstract: Urothelial carcinoma (UC) often exhibits a "cold" tumor microenvironment with limited immune cell infiltration, leading to resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors. Neutral sphingomyelinase (nSMase) is a key regulator of extracellular vesicle (EV) biogenesis, and pharmacological inhibition of nSMase using GW4869 has been widely used to modulate EV biogenesis. However, its impact on EV dynamics and anti-tumor immunity remains unclear. Using the syngeneic murine UC cell line, MBT-2, we assessed the effects of GW4869 on gene expression and protein secretion using RNA sequencing and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. Natural killer (NK) cell function was evaluated using lactate dehydrogenase cytotoxicity assays and CD107a degranulation analysis, and public datasets were analyzed to examine the clinical relevance of C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 10 (CXCL10) expression in human UC. GW4869 treatment was associated with altered EV dynamics, characterized by increased particle yields and changes in EV size distribution. Functional assays demonstrated that GW4869-treated tumor cells enhanced NK cell-mediated cytotoxicity and degranulation, and this anti-tumor effect was augmented by programmed cell death ligand 1 (PD-L1) blockade. These effects were attenuated by C-X-C motif chemokine receptor 3 (CXCR3) neutralization, suggesting the involvement of the CXCL10-CXCR3 axis. Clinically, high CXCL10 expression was associated with favorable survival outcomes and positively correlated with NK cell-associated markers in patients with UC. In conclusion, pharmacological nSMase inhibition modulates EV and secretome dynamics and promotes NK cell activation associated with the CXCL10-CXCR3 axis. These findings support further investigation of nSMase-targeted strategies for enhancing anti-tumor immunity in UC.

title: In silico characterization of the protein Aβ175 from circular RNA CircAβ-a and its involvement in the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease (AD).
abstract: Circular RNAs are specialized single-stranded molecules having covalently closed termini. They were once thought to be mere transcriptional artefacts. However, they have now been identified as significant players in tumorigenesis, neurodegeneration and other diseases. Though generally classified as non-coding, certain circular RNAs demonstrate the ability to encode proteins, reshaping our understanding of their biological roles. CircAβ-a, a circRNA that contains the amyloid beta (Aβ)-coding region of the APP gene, acts as an alternative source of Aβ peptides. The discovery of circAβ-a suggests that Aβ peptides can be generated through a non-canonical translation mechanism, independent of APP processing and that Aβ peptides are the key contributors to Alzheimer's Disease pathogenesis. CircAβ-a is efficiently translated into Aβ175, which is further processed into Aβ peptides. Inhibiting circAβ-a translation or modifying its expression might help in reducing Aβ accumulation in brain. To develop effective inhibitors for Aβ peptides, it is crucial to understand its structural characteristics, functional properties and interaction patterns. This study focuses on characterizing the Aβ175 protein by predicting its structural features to explore its potential as an alternative biomarker, which can be verified through wet-lab experiments, for the treatment of Alzheimer's Disease.

title: The venom-gland small RNA transcriptome of the centipede Scolopendra subspinipes mutilans across the venom-release cycle.
abstract: Venom production in centipedes is cyclical, but the small RNA content of the venom gland and its changes across the venom-release cycle have not been described. We sequenced nine small RNA libraries from venom glands of Scolopendra subspinipes mutilans, three at each of three stages: before release, and 0 h and 1 h after electrically induced venom release, and analysed the deposited reads with an open pipeline. miRNAs accounted for 47.6-65.2% of reads. Reads matched 52 conserved miRNA families with arthropod members, including the mandibulate-specific miR-965 and miR-282 and miR-125, which has not been found in the genome of the centipede Strigamia maritima. Reads of 24-30 nt outside known non-coding RNA classes made up 8.4-25.9% of each library; they were biased towards a 5' uridine, showed a strong ping-pong signature and, in a post hoc analysis, came preferentially from transcripts resembling transposable-element proteins, indicating piRNA-like small RNAs in this somatic tissue. No miRNA unit met the differential-abundance criteria of both DESeq2 and edgeR. For 53-65 of 272 miRNA units per comparison, the confidence interval excluded changes of two-fold or more, and simulations indicated that three libraries per stage detect a two-fold change with 14% power. novel-miR34, a predicted novel miRNA whose precursor lies within a transcript annotated as a CAP-superfamily venom allergen, was not significantly altered. A survey of 9,485 NCBI protein records annotated as venom allergens showed that this label is applied across many taxa. These data provide a replicated small RNA resource for a myriapod venom gland.

title: Applications of dendrimers for prostate cancer gene therapy: current status and future perspectives.
abstract: Prostate cancer remains a major global health burden, and metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer remains incurable despite advances in systemic therapy. Gene and RNA therapeutics offer opportunities to target mechanisms that are difficult to modulate conventionally, but their translation is limited by delivery. Dendrimers are highly branched, generation-defined macromolecules that can condense and protect nucleic acids and be engineered with targeting ligands, steric stabilizers and stimuli-responsive components. This review critically evaluates dendrimer-based gene therapy for prostate cancer through an evidence-to-translation framework that separates direct therapeutic, platform and contextual evidence, while drawing selectively on the broader dendrimer literature to inform mechanism, design and translation. PAMAM and diaminobutyric poly(propylene imine) dendrimers dominate the field, with peptide dendrimers, dendrimersomes and hybrid nanomaterials expanding the design space. Reported therapeutic cargoes include siRNAs targeting Hsp27, BIRC5/survivin, cofilin-1 and MCL-1, plasmid-encoded MEG3, and cytokine-encoding plasmids. Although active targeting and systemic delivery have produced encouraging preclinical efficacy, major barriers remain, including serum instability, inefficient intracellular unpacking, limited biodistribution and pharmacokinetic data, cationic toxicity, and inadequate repeat-dose safety studies. Future progress will require biodegradable or ionizable architectures, clinically relevant metastatic models, biomarker-informed targeting, functional biodistribution, and scalable manufacturing.

title: Cerium-polyphenol network protects against AMD-associated RPE degeneration via blood-retinal barrier immunomodulation.
abstract: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) remains difficult to treat due to the complex pathogenesis of retinal microenvironment (RME). In this study, we developed a cerium-rhein network encapsulated with polyvinylpyrrolidone (CRP NPs) to enhance biocompatibility. CRP NPs exhibited robust catalase (CAT)- and superoxide dismutase (SOD)-like activities and modulated the immune microenvironment within blood-retinal barrier (BRB). In vitro, CRP NPs protected ARPE-19 cells from NaIO3-induced damage and preserved BRB integrity by upregulating tight junction proteins and transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER). Mechanistic studies using RNA-seq, western blotting, and molecular docking revealed that rhein released from NPs inhibits the receptor for advanced glycation end products (RAGE) signaling pathway. Together with the reactive oxygen species (ROS)-scavenging activity of cerium (Ce3+/4+), this effect contributed to the suppression of ferroptotic cell death and attenuates the "HMGB1-RAGE-ROS-ferroptosis-HMGB1" vicious cycle. Besides, CRP NPs shifted microglia from a pro-inflammatory activation to an anti-inflammatory phenotype by reducing the release of high mobility group box-1 protein (HMGB1) and calreticulin (CALR). This immunomodulation led to remodeling of the RME, as evidenced by reduced levels of IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, and COX2. In a NaIO3-induced dry AMD-like degeneration mouse model, treatment with CRP NPs significantly preserved RPE, improved visual function, and restored BRB integrity. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that CRP NPs present a multimodal therapeutic platform for AMD-like retinal degeneration, acting through immunomodulation of the RME and inhibition of ferroptosis in retinal pigment epithelium.

title: The Mechanism of Montelukast Sodium to Improve Inflammation in Ischemic Stroke: Based on Astroglia-Microglia Interactions.
abstract: The present study aimed to elucidate the neuroprotective mechanism of montelukast sodium (MS) in ischemic stroke, with particular emphasis on astrocyte-microglia interactions. In vivo, adult male mice (n = 10/group) were subjected to distal middle cerebral artery occlusion (dMCAO) and then intraperitoneally injected with MS (4 mg/kg) or an equivalent volume of saline for 7 consecutive days. In vitro, primary mouse astrocytes and microglia were isolated and co-cultured, then exposed to oxygen-glucose deprivation and reoxygenation (OGD/R) to mimic ischemic-reperfusion injury. Prior to MS intervention, astrocytes were transfected with HMGB1 overexpression plasmid (oeHMGB1) or short hairpin RNA against HMGB1 (shHMGB1) to overexpress or knock down HMGB1, or treated with an anti-HMGB1 antibody in the co-culture system. Primary outcomes included infarct volume (TTC staining), microglia activation (immunofluorescence), M1/M2-associated markers in microglia (RT-qPCR, immunofluorescence), S100 calcium-binding protein beta (S100β) levels, inflammatory mediators, and HMGB1/TLR4/NF-κB pathway activity (immunohistochemistry, RT-qPCR, Western Blot). MS administration reduced the cerebral infarction size in dMCAO mice, attenuated the upregulation of S100β and ROS levels, and suppressed HMGB1/TLR4/NF-κB signaling cascade in vivo. In the co-culture system, conditioned medium from MS-treated astrocytes promoted microglial polarization toward an M2-associated phenotype, as evidenced by increased Arg-1/CD206/IL-10 and decreased iNOS/TNF-α/CD16. The protective effects of MS were reversed by HMGB1 overexpression, but potentiated by HMGB1 neutralization. Crucially, pharmacological inhibition of TLR4 with TAK-242 mimicked the effects of MS, while the combination of MS and TAK-242 produced no additional benefits. Collectively, MS confers neuroprotection against cerebral ischemic injury by inhibiting HMGB1/TLR4/NF-κB signaling pathway and promoting microglial polarization.

title: Disuse enhances cancellous and cortical bone responses to mechanical loading by altering lacunocanalicular fluid dynamics.
abstract: Disuse conditions, such as microgravity, prolonged bed rest, sedentary lifestyle, and limb immobilization, frequently affect human skeletal responses to mechanical loading. However, the precise impact of disuse on bone adaptation to mechanical loading and its underlying mechanobiological mechanisms remain unclear. Osteocytes are recognized as the primary mechanosensors within the fluid dynamic microenvironment of the lacunocanalicular network (LCN). Given that disuse can significantly alter LCN structure, we hypothesized that disuse would influence cancellous and cortical bone responses to mechanical loading by modifying lacunocanalicular fluid dynamics. To test this hypothesis, we employed a combination of in vivo animal experiments, whole bone-LCN multi-scale modeling, and RNA-sequencing. By applying identical in vivo axial loading to tibiae of hindlimb unloading and ground control mice, we observed that disuse enhanced loading-induced changes in cancellous and cortical bone mass and mechanical properties. Furthermore, we discovered that disuse increased lacunar volumes in both cancellous and cortical bone, thereby enhancing the loading-induced fluid dynamic microenvironment (e.g., fluid shear stress [FSS]) for osteocytes and promoting activation of downstream FSS-related signaling pathways. These findings underscore the importance of the mechanical microenvironment of osteocytes within the LCN in regulating bone adaptive responses to mechanical loading. This study advances our understanding of bone mechanoadaptation, particularly under disuse conditions.

title: Chromosome-level genome assembly of the Korean wheat cultivar Keumkang.
abstract: Bread wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) cultivar Keumkang is a major winter wheat grown across the Korean Peninsula, where its early heading, strong adaptation to temperate monsoon climates, and desirable grain quality make it a central genotype in regional breeding programs. Here, we report a high quality, chromosome-scale reference genome assembly for T. aestivum cv. Keumkang (Keumkang v1.1). Using PacBio HiFi, Oxford Nanopore, and Omni-C sequencing, we assembled a 14.54 Gb genome with a contig N50 of 79.13 Mb after removing organelle reads prior to assembly. The assembly exhibits high completeness, with 98.81% of BUSCO genes detected. Comprehensive gene annotation integrating PacBio Iso-Seq, Illumina RNA-Seq, protein homology, gene projection, and ab initio predictions identified 255,293 gene models, including 145,082 high confidence (HC) and 110,211 low confidence (LC) genes. As the first chromosome-scale genome generated for a commercially cultivated Asian wheat variety, Keumkang v1.1 provides a valuable genomic resource for dissecting agronomic traits, supporting regional breeding efforts, and advancing comparative genomics in hexaploid wheat.

title: Machine learning-guided drug repurposing identifies potential CDK1 inhibitors for glioblastoma: An integrative transcriptomic and molecular simulation study.
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) remains one of the most lethal and therapeutically challenging tumors of the central nervous system with limited treatment options and a poor survival rate. The identification of clinically important molecular targets and new drug candidates is required to improve GBM management. In the current study, an integrated computational framework merging multi-transcriptomic analysis, network biology, machine learning, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics simulations was employed to explore potential therapeutic targets and repurposable drugs for GBM. Five independent GBM transcriptomic datasets from microarray and RNA-sequencing profiles were analyzed to identify consistently dysregulated genes in GBM. Protein-protein interaction network analysis and hub gene prioritization revealed cyclin-dependent kinase 1 (CDK1) as a central regulatory gene associated with GBM progression. An ML-based drug-repurposing approach was applied to identify potential CDK1 inhibitors using experimentally validated protein bioactivity data from the CHEMBL database. Among the 40 models, the XGBoost regression model showed best performance (R2 =0.74) and was subsequently applied to screen an FDA-approved drug library containing 1615 compounds. Following ADMET and blood-brain barrier permeability assessment, 122 candidates were subjected to molecular docking. Risperidone and butorphanol exhibited the strongest binding affinities toward CDK1, with docking scores of -9.3 and -9.1 kcal/mol, respectively. Subsequent 200 ns molecular dynamics simulations indicated that both complexes remained structurally stable, with backbone RMSD values below 5 Å and stable radius of gyration throughout the trajectories. The CDK1- risperidone complex exhibited lower and more consistent backbone deviation (RMSD 3.09 ± 0.19 Å) and greater compactness (Rg 20.42 ± 0.16 Å), whereas the CDK1-Butorphanol complex maintained more persistent hydrogen bonding and a marginally more favorable MM-GBSA binding free energy (-45.12 ± 3.62 kcal/mol versus -42.20 ± 3.69 kcal/mol for risperidone). Overall, this study identifies CDK1 as a potential therapeutic vulnerability in GBM and highlights risperidone and butorphanol as promising repurposing candidates warranting further experimental validation.

title: AGR3 drives M1 polarization and glycolytic reprogramming of pulmonary macrophages via stabilizing HIF-1α/PKM2 axis to aggravate CLP-induced sepsis-associated acute respiratory distress syndrome.
abstract: Sepsis-associated acute respiratory distress syndrome (sepsis-ARDS) remains a life-threatening critical illness with limited targeted therapeutics, where pulmonary macrophage M1 polarization and aerobic glycolysis act as core drivers of inflammatory lung injury. Anterior gradient 3 (AGR3), an endoplasmic reticulum disulfide isomerase, was recently identified as a dysregulated transcript in human ARDS patient datasets, yet its immunometabolic function in septic lung injury remains undefined. Here, we aimed to characterize the role and molecular cascade of AGR3 in regulating macrophage polarization and glycolytic reprogramming during polymicrobial sepsis, combining the in vivo CLP septic mouse model with an in vitro LPS/IFN-γ-induced M1 polarization model in RAW264.7 macrophages. Bioinformatic mining of GSE66890 RNA-seq dataset revealed prominent AGR3 upregulation in human ARDS lung tissues, which we validated in cecal ligation and puncture (CLP)-induced septic mouse lungs and LPS/IFN-γ-stimulated RAW264.7 macrophages. Lentiviral-mediated AGR3 knockdown suppressed M1 macrophage polarization, reduced glycolytic flux (lower ECAR, higher OCR, diminished lactate secretion), and blunted pro-inflammatory cytokine release in vitro. Mechanistic biochemistry assays demonstrated that AGR3 physically interacts with hypoxia-inducible factor 1α (HIF-1α), extending HIF-1α protein half-life by restraining proteasomal degradation and promoting its nuclear translocation. Chromatin immunoprecipitation confirmed that stabilized nuclear HIF-1α transcriptionally activates pyruvate kinase M2 (Pkm2), a master glycolytic effector. Reciprocal rescue experiments verified that ectopic overexpression of HIF-1α or PKM2 largely reversed the anti-inflammatory, metabolic phenotypes induced by AGR3 silencing. In vivo intratracheal AAV9-shAGR3 delivery mitigated CLP-triggered pulmonary edema, neutrophil infiltration, M1 macrophage accumulation, and restored protective PKM2 tetramer formation, accompanied by significant improvement in pulmonary function and 7-day survival of septic mice. Taken together, AGR3 mediates sepsis-induced lung injury via the HIF-1α/PKM2 signaling. This study provides a novel potential therapeutic target for sepsis-associated ARDS.

title: Transcriptional Landscape of Immune Cells and Key Gene Expression in Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma: A Single-Cell RNA Sequencing Approach.
abstract: Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) is a common malignancy with considerable heterogeneity and complex interactions within the tumor microenvironment. Information about the transcriptional heterogeneity of immune cells and expression profiles of important genes can shed light on disease progression and identify potential therapeutic targets. We employed single-cell RNA sequencing to characterize the immune cell landscape in ESCC. We analyzed cellular composition and transcriptional heterogeneity using dimensionality reduction methodologies including UMAP and t-SNE. To further identify active biological processes and signaling pathways in the immune microenvironment, we determined Gene Ontology (GO) and pathway enrichment. We identified a complex structure of immune cell subpopulations, demonstrating distinct transcriptional patterns. Specific expression patterns of some key genes were evident among the cell types, including high expression in regulatory T cells and natural killer T cells. The SPP1 signaling pathway emerged as a potentially important candidate in computationally inferred immune cell communication. Pseudotime analysis showed dynamic changes in representative gene expression, indicating transcriptional state variation. The complex immune response in the ESCC microenvironment is revealed in this study through the exploration of immune cells and key gene activity at single-cell transcriptional resolution. This knowledge may help guide the development of personalized immunotherapies by revealing the roles of specific immune cells and potential therapeutic targets.

title: Integrative bulk and single-cell transcriptomic analysis identifies a PLAUR-centered macrophage-associated programmed cell death signature in type A aortic dissection.
abstract: Type A aortic dissection (TAAD) is a life-threatening aortic emergency characterized by inflammatory remodeling, extracellular matrix disruption, and programmed cell death (PCD). The cell-specific transcriptional features associated with immune activation and PCD-related aortic wall injury remain incompletely defined. This study investigated PCD-associated immune remodeling in TAAD and evaluated PLAUR as a macrophage-associated marker linked to these pathological changes. Public bulk transcriptomic datasets were integrated with single-cell RNA sequencing, curated PCD-related gene sets, immune deconvolution, pathway enrichment, in silico perturbation analysis, and histological assessment of human aortic specimens. TAAD tissues exhibited marked transcriptomic alterations, with 2,217 genes meeting the exploratory differential-expression criteria, accompanied by increased PCD-related transcriptional activity. Single-cell analysis indicated that macrophage-enriched clusters showed relatively high PCD-related gene-set activity, while PLAUR transcripts were predominantly detected in macrophage-enriched clusters. PLAUR was upregulated in TAAD in both training and external validation datasets and strongly correlated with sample-level PCD scores. In the training dataset, PLAUR expression showed exploratory discrimination between TAAD and control tissue samples, with an AUC of 0.858. PLAUR-high samples showed enrichment of HIF-1, JAK-STAT, necroptosis, and apoptosis-related pathways. Immune deconvolution indicated relatively higher neutrophil- and M0 macrophage-associated signatures in TAAD, with PLAUR expression positively associated with myeloid-cell-related features. In silico perturbation analysis identified cytoskeletal and actin-related transcriptional changes associated with predicted PLAUR perturbation. Histological assessment demonstrated aortic wall disorganization, collagen remodeling, elastic fiber disruption, increased TUNEL positivity, and elevated PLAUR protein expression in TAAD lesions. PLAUR is associated with macrophage-enriched inflammatory, proteolytic, and PCD-related remodeling in TAAD and may serve as a candidate marker of these pathological features. The present findings are associative and do not establish a causal role for PLAUR in aortic wall degeneration or dissection initiation. Spatially resolved and functional studies are required to determine whether PLAUR-positive macrophage states contribute mechanistically to TAAD pathogenesis.

title: Neuron-enriched STAT4 shapes time- and context-dependent neuronal outcomes in Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Neuronal dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease (AD) is increasingly linked to dynamic and context-dependent alterations in intracellular signaling. However, how these changes drive progressive neurodegeneration and divergent neuronal outcomes remains poorly understood. Integrative analyses across independent human single-nucleus RNA sequencing datasets were performed to identify neuronal factors consistently altered in AD. Signal transducer and activator of transcription 4 (STAT4) distribution in different cell types was further validated using a mouse single-cell RNA sequencing dataset and experimental models. Functions of STAT4 were examined in human SH-SY5Y cells, mouse HT22 neuronal cells, mouse primary neurons, and inducible systems. In vivo effects were assessed in 3×Tg-AD and wild-type mice with AAV-mediated Stat4 modulation and pharmacological ERK inhibition. Multi-omics approaches, including RNA-seq, Cut&Tag, and RIP-seq, were used to explore downstream regulatory mechanisms. Integrative analyses identified STAT4 as a neuron-enriched factor consistently reduced in AD neurons. STAT4 supported neuronal integrity and synaptic homeostasis under basal conditions. Inducible restoration of STAT4 expression exerted divergent effects in a time-dependent manner, with early adaptive responses transitioning to later oxidative stress- and apoptosis-associated changes. Sustained STAT4 restoration induced oxidative stress, apoptosis-related signaling, and tau protein-related alterations, which were attenuated by ERK inhibition. In contrast, the beneficial outputs, including reduced Aβ burden and improved synaptic and neuronal markers, were preserved despite ERK inhibition. Parallel analyses in wild-type mice showed a delayed trajectory, indicating disease-context-dependent modulation. STAT4 was further associated with coordinated signaling networks and hnRNPK-related regulatory complexes. These findings define a time- and context-dependent signaling framework in which STAT4-associated outputs progressively shift toward maladaptive, ERK-sensitive responses in AD. Selective constraint of the late-stage signaling imbalance may attenuate the pathological outcomes while preserving the beneficial effects, providing a potential strategy for context-specific therapeutic intervention.

title: Integrative genomic analysis reveals candidate genes and potential molecular mechanisms in carotid atherosclerosis.
abstract: Carotid intima-media thickness and carotid plaque are key ultrasound-derived indicators of subclinical carotid atherosclerosis. However, the shared genetic architecture linking arterial wall remodeling and plaque formation remains incompletely understood. We integrated summary-level genome-wide association study data for common carotid artery intima-media thickness and carotid plaque using N-weighted multivariate genome-wide association meta-analysis. Significant loci were annotated with FUMA platform. Candidate genes were prioritized using positional mapping, transcriptome-wide association analysis, multi-marker analysis of genomic annotation, and summary-data-based Mendelian randomization combined with the heterogeneity in dependent instruments analysis. Gene ontology enrichment, single-nucleus RNA sequencing, target tractability assessment, and protein network analysis were performed for functional interpretation. Independent gene-level and experimental validation were subsequently performed to further support the prioritized findings. The multivariate analysis identified 12 genome-wide significant loci associated with the shared genetic component of carotid intima-media thickness and carotid plaque. Four complementary prioritization strategies prioritized 31 non-redundant candidate genes. BCAR1 showed the most consistent statistical support across all four methods, while SOX7 and TMEM170A were supported by multiple approaches. Functional enrichment highlighted lipid and lipoprotein metabolism, whereas single-nucleus RNA sequencing showed preferential enrichment of BCAR1 in vascular smooth muscle cells. Independent gene-level and experimental validation further supported BCAR1, with significant external gene-level association and functional effects of BCAR1 knockdown on oxidized low-density lipoprotein-induced vascular smooth muscle cells responses. By integrating the shared genetic architecture of cIMT and carotid plaque with complementary gene-prioritization, cell-type-resolved, independent gene-level, and functional evidence, this study prioritizes BCAR1 as a genetically supported candidate gene for carotid atherosclerosis. These findings provide a biological and cellular framework for further mechanistic investigation.

title: Genetic analyses prioritize a candidate peripheral ferroptosis-related immune-protein network in migraine.
abstract: Migraine is a disabling neurological disorder with substantial clinical heterogeneity. Ferroptosis-annotated genes encompass functions related to iron and redox homeostasis, lipid peroxidation, and immune regulation, but the genetically supported relationships connecting these processes with peripheral immune-cell phenotypes and circulating proteins have not been systematically examined. We integrated summary-data-based Mendelian randomization, two-sample Mendelian randomization, colocalization analysis, indirect-effect analysis, PBMC single-cell RNA sequencing, and druggability annotation. Five migraine genome-wide association study datasets were analyzed; GCST90043743 included 166 cases and was treated as a sensitivity dataset. A set of 718 ferroptosis-related genes was evaluated using blood mQTL and eQTL resources and plasma pQTL datasets, while immune-cell MR included 731 immunophenotypes. Evidence was first assessed across molecular data types and migraine outcomes and was then integrated with immune-cell traits, circulating proteins, single-cell expression context, and druggability information. Thirteen genes met the highest cross-omics evidence criteria: ACADSB, ADAMTS13, CDH1, CHMP1A, DPP4, GCH1, GSTM1, ISCU, MAPK9, MAPK14, MUC1, TFRC, and TLR4. A further 25 genes showed recurrent but incomplete cross-omics evidence. Of 2,087 colocalization tests, 313 met the colocalization support criterion, and all 13 highest-evidence genes had at least one result meeting this criterion. Immune-cell MR identified recurrent CD27-related B-cell and CD33-related myeloid traits. Thirty-four matched results from the two indirect-effect analyses were retained; 22 shared CD27-related B-cell traits between GSTM1- or TFRC-related gene-side results and ENPP2-related protein-side results. Additional matched results involved MUC1, myeloid dendritic-cell or naive CD8bright T-cell traits, and HMOX1 or IDO1; ALOX15, CD38-related B-cell or activated Treg traits, and IL1B; and CISD2, a CD27-related B-cell trait, and IFNG. PBMC single-cell RNA sequencing provided peripheral cell-type expression context, and targeted pseudobulk analysis showed increased IFNG expression in CD8+ T cells after Bonferroni correction. Druggability annotation highlighted ENPP2, IDO1, IL1B, and IFNG for translational follow-up. This study prioritizes a candidate peripheral ferroptosis-related immune-protein network associated with migraine susceptibility. The most recurrent relationship involved GSTM1 or TFRC, CD27-related B-cell traits, and ENPP2, with additional myeloid, B-cell/Treg, and inflammatory components. These findings nominate genetically informed candidates for biomarker research, immune-metabolic stratification, and experimental target investigation in migraine.

title: Genome Sequencing and Analysis for Assessing Genetic Disease Risk: AI-Driven Frontiers and Breakthrough Directions.
abstract: Recent advances at the intersection of artificial intelligence (AI) and genomics are transforming approaches to assessing genetic disease risk. The scale and complexity of genomic, transcriptomic, and related datasets demand methods capable of integrating information across multiple modalities while preserving biological context. This review begins with the emerging concept of the "genomic language paradigm," which frames DNA and RNA sequences as structured codes interpretable by large-scale machine learning models. We then examine the use of graph neural networks to map molecular interaction networks and attention-based methods for detecting functionally important noncoding elements. Approaches that bring together multi-omics resources and longitudinal data are discussed for their ability to reveal how diseases unfold over time. Interpretability is considered in relation to the shift from observing statistical patterns to uncovering causal mechanisms, alongside privacy-preserving strategies such as federated learning that make it possible for institutions to work with sensitive genomic data without exchanging raw files. We also look at developments that could extend AI-enabled genomics into everyday clinical practice, such as on-site analysis through edge computing, and experimental computing architectures that may accelerate large-scale modeling. Finally, we outline factors that will shape clinical adoption-not only regulatory approval, but also the practical challenge of embedding these tools into established healthcare systems. The trajectory of these innovations suggests a move toward genomic medicine that is more predictive, personally relevant, and available to a wider range of patients.

title: Integrated transcriptomic and proteomic profiling of RXRA-overexpressing chronic myeloid leukemia cells identifies protein kinase D as a candidate target for imatinib sensitization.
abstract: Retinoid-X-receptor alpha (RXRA) is downregulated in chronic myeloid leukemia (CML). We previously demonstrated that overexpression of RXRA sensitizes CML cells to imatinib, but the mechanisms underlying this effect remain undefined. To characterize the molecular programs associated with RXRA-mediated imatinib sensitization through integrated transcriptomic-proteomic profiling, and to identify and examine pharmacologically actionable downstream effectors in CML cell lines and primary patient-derived CD34+ cells. RXRA-overexpressing (RXRA-OE) and empty vector (EV) LAMA84 cells were profiled by RNA sequencing and mass spectrometry-based proteomics. Four concordantly downregulated candidates (PRKD1, UCHL1, FSCN1 and NTRK3), prioritized by magnitude of concordant downregulation, biological relevance and inhibitor availability, were confirmed by qRT-PCR and immunoblotting. Pharmacological inhibition of each candidate combined with imatinib was assessed in CML cell lines, primary CML CD34+ cells and healthy-donor CD34+ controls. RXRA overexpression produced 7,053 differentially expressed transcripts and 1,668 differentially abundant proteins (technical triplicates of one sample per group), with 711 concordant gene-protein pairs (Pearson r = 0.64). RXRA-overexpressing cells scored higher for genes downregulated in hematopoietic stem cells and for the granulocyte-monocyte progenitor signature, with enriched myeloid gene sets and reduced expression of receptor tyrosine kinase and growth-factor signaling genes. Enzymes of glycolysis, the pentose phosphate pathway and sterol biosynthesis were downregulated, while lipid catabolic genes were upregulated. Among the four candidates, the serine/threonine kinase PRKD1 and the deubiquitinase UCHL1 emerged as candidate imatinib-sensitizing targets: the pan-PKD inhibitor CRT0066101 and the UCHL1 inhibitor LDN-57444 each synergized with imatinib and reduced clonogenic potential. PRKD1 protein was detected in all four CML cell lines tested. Combined PKD inhibition and imatinib reduced the viability and colony-forming capacity of primary CML CD34+ cells. In healthy-donor CD34+ cells the live-cell fraction did not differ between treatments (n = 5), and colony formation was assessed in two donors; these comparisons were limited by sample size and selectivity for CML cells was not established. Integrated multi-omics associates RXRA overexpression with myeloid lineage-associated and metabolic expression signatures in imatinib-sensitized CML cells, and identifies PRKD1 as a candidate effector whose pharmacological targeting with a pan-PKD inhibitor enhances imatinib efficacy in vitro.

title: Salidroside decreases lipid abundance, mitochondrial function, and expression of the mitochondrial citrate transporter SLC25A1 via miR-1343-3p in gastric cancer.
abstract: To investigate the potential mechanisms by which salidroside regulates mitochondrial function, SLC25A1 expression, and lipid abundance in gastric cancer (GC) cells via miR-1343-3p. Transcriptome sequencing was performed on MGC-803 cells before and after salidroside treatment to identify differentially expressed miRNAs and mRNAs. Bioinformatic analysis was then used to screen for candidate molecules. The interaction between miR-1343-3p and SLC25A1 was validated by dual-luciferase reporter assay, sequence alignment, and RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP). Mitochondrial morphology and function were examined by transmission electron microscopy and fluorescent probes. MGC-803 and AGS cells were used to assess the effects of salidroside, miR-1343-3p modulation, and SLC25A1 silencing on mitochondrial citrate export, lipid abundance, and cell proliferation. Furthermore, a nude mouse xenograft model was established to evaluate the effects of salidroside and a miR-1343-3p agomir on tumor growth, the expression of miR-1343-3p and SLC25A1, and tumor metabolic status. Transcriptome sequencing revealed 44 differentially expressed miRNAs and 1,384 differentially expressed mRNAs in MGC-803 cells following salidroside treatment. Among them, miR-1343-3p was significantly upregulated as a tumor-suppressive miRNA, while SLC25A1, a mitochondrial citrate transporter, was significantly downregulated. RT-qPCR and Western blot results demonstrated that salidroside significantly increased the expression of miR-1343-3p while decreasing the mRNA and protein expression of SLC25A1. Dual-luciferase reporter, sequence alignment, and RIP assays confirmed that miR-1343-3p directly targets SLC25A1. Further studies showed that salidroside treatment, miR-1343-3p overexpression, and SLC25A1 silencing could all cause the accumulation of mitochondrial citrate, reduced mitochondrial membrane potential, increased ROS production, and decreased the levels of NADH, ATP, acetyl-CoA, free fatty acids, cholesterol, and triglycerides, while significantly inhibiting GC cell proliferation. However, after knocking down miR-1343-3p, the opposite results were observed, which were efficiently rescued by salidroside. In vivo, both salidroside treatment and the miR-1343-3p agomir administration significantly reduced tumor volume and weight. Tumor tissues from these groups showed increased miR-1343-3p expression, decreased SLC25A1 expression, and lipid metabolic changes consistent with those observed in vitro. Salidroside inhibits GC cell proliferation and tumor growth by upregulating the tumor-suppressive miR-1343-3p, which directly targets and downregulates the mitochondrial citrate transporter SLC25A1. Meanwhile, decreased mitochondrial citrate export, impaired mitochondrial function, and reduced lipid abundance are observed. These findings indicate that miR-1343-3p and SLC25A1 may be promising therapeutic targets for metabolic intervention in gastric cancer.

title: Mapping the NFYA 3'UTR landscape identifies alternative polyadenylation as a targetable vulnerability in prostate cancer.
abstract: Alternative polyadenylation (APA) is increasingly recognized as a pervasive oncogenic mechanism that reshapes post-transcriptional gene regulation and promotes tumor aggressiveness. Whether APA contributes to the dysregulation of NFYA-encoding the regulatory subunit of the oncogenic transcription factor NF-Y-in prostate cancer (PCa) remains largely uncharacterized. We interrogated bulk, single cell and 3'-end RNA-sequencing data from PCa cell lines and patient samples to re-annotate and quantify the usage of NFYA 3'UTRs. The functional consequences of APA were assessed using reporter assays. NFYA APA was experimentally reprogrammed using CRISPR/Cas9-mediated deletion and antisense oligonucleotide (ASO)-based masking of polyadenylation signals, followed by in vitro and in vivo phenotypic analyses. Four functional NFYA 3'UTR isoforms were identified, with one predominantly used across cell lines and tissues. PCa displayed pervasive NFYA 3'UTR shortening, which correlated with tumor grade and metastatic disease, increased NF-YA protein abundance, and enhanced proliferation. 3'UTR lengthening was instead observed upon induction of cellular quiescence or after Enzalutamide treatment.
